name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Route all zero-speech videos to curation immediately. This cuts noise early by flagging silent uploads for human review before they waste downstream resources. The trade-off is a slight delay for creators, but it prevents false positives from clogging the pipeline. Ingestion owns this—no other team can act faster.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s plan risks overloading curation with false positives—silent videos could be intentional (e.g., ambient soundscapes, ASMR). Instead, route only videos with *zero audio track* to curation; flag others for creator confirmation first. Ingestion and curation should co-own the rule, with a 24-hour trial to measure false-positive rate.

name: Chisel
text:
Route all videos with a *zero audio track* directly to curation for human review. This cuts false positives from intentional silence (ASMR, soundscapes) while still catching accidental uploads early. The trade-off is a small uptick in curation workload, but it prevents wasted downstream processing on clearly broken files. Ingestion owns the rule; curation handles the review.
[dispatched 3 workers: worker-9357, worker-9737, worker-9024 — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s plan still risks overloading curation with borderline cases—videos with near-zero audio (e.g., 1-second ambient noise) will trigger human review for no reason. Better: route only videos with *confirmed zero audio track* (not just "zero" flag) to curation, and let ingestion auto-flag the rest for creator confirmation. Settle it with a 48-hour test: measure curation load before/after, and creator response rates to the confirmation prompt.

name: Scope
text: Route only videos with a *confirmed zero audio track*—no flags, no near-zero guesses—to curation immediately. This kills false positives from intentional silence (ASMR, soundscapes) while still catching accidental uploads early. The trade-off is a one-time engineering cost to verify the audio track exists before routing, but it saves curation from drowning in borderline cases. Ingestion owns the check; curation gets clean, actionable inputs.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s plan still risks under-catching accidental uploads—confirmed zero audio tracks could miss videos where audio exists but is corrupted or inaudible. Instead, route videos with *audio track present but empty* (confirmed via metadata) to curation, and let ingestion auto-flag the rest for creator confirmation. A 48-hour A/B test comparing false positives and creator friction will settle it.

name: Reel
text: Route only videos with a *confirmed empty audio track* (verified via metadata, not just flags) to curation immediately. This catches accidental silent uploads early while avoiding false positives from intentional silence (ASMR, soundscapes) or near-zero audio. The trade-off is a small engineering cost to validate the audio track, but it prevents wasted downstream processing and curation overload. Ingestion owns the verification—no other team.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s plan still risks missing videos where audio is present but unusable—corrupted, inaudible, or non-English speech—while over-flagging intentional silence. Instead, route videos with *audio track present but flagged as "silent" by ingestion* to curation, and let ingestion auto-flag the rest for creator confirmation. The lead should decide by testing both rules on a 1,000-video sample and measuring false positives vs. missed accidental uploads.

name: Chisel
text: Route videos with an *audio track flagged as "silent" by ingestion* directly to curation. This catches accidental silent uploads early while avoiding false positives from intentional silence (ASMR, soundscapes) or near-zero audio. The trade-off is missing some corrupted or inaudible audio cases, but it balances accuracy and workload better than stricter or looser rules.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s "silent" flag risks missing videos where audio is present but unusable—corrupted, inaudible, or non-English speech—while over-flagging intentional silence. Instead, route videos with *audio track present but flagged as "empty" by ingestion* to curation, and let ingestion auto-flag the rest for creator review. Settle it with a test: compare false positives (ASMR/soundscapes) and false negatives (corrupted audio) between the two approaches over a week of live traffic.

name: Scope
text: Route videos with an *audio track confirmed empty by ingestion* directly to curation. This catches accidental silent uploads early while avoiding false positives from intentional silence (ASMR, soundscapes) or near-zero audio. The trade-off is missing some corrupted or inaudible audio cases, but ingestion’s metadata check is faster and more reliable than manual flagging. Engineering implements the empty-audio check in the ingestion pipeline—no extra steps.

name: Scriv
text: The "confirmed empty" flag still risks missing videos where audio exists but is unusable—corrupted, inaudible, or non-English speech—while over-flagging intentional silence. Instead, route videos with *audio track present but flagged as "silent" by ingestion* to curation, and let ingestion auto-flag the rest for creator review. The real risk is under-catching corrupted audio; settle it by testing ingestion’s "silent" detection against a labeled dataset of corrupted/inaudible clips.

name: Reel
text: Route videos with an *audio track flagged as "silent" by ingestion* directly to curation. This catches accidental silent uploads early while avoiding false positives from intentional silence (ASMR, soundscapes) or near-zero audio. The trade-off is missing some corrupted or inaudible audio cases, but ingestion’s "silent" flag is the most reliable signal we have without overcomplicating the pipeline.

name: Scriv
text: The "silent" flag still risks missing videos where audio exists but is unusable—corrupted, inaudible, or non-English speech—while over-flagging intentional silence. Instead, route videos with *audio track present but flagged as "untranscribed" by ingestion* to curation, and let ingestion auto-flag the rest. The lead for this is ingestion engineering; settle the argument by testing the "untranscribed" flag against a labeled dataset of edge cases.

name: Chisel
text: Route videos with an *audio track flagged as "untranscribed" by ingestion* directly to curation. This catches the widest range of unusable audio—corrupted, inaudible, or non-English speech—without over-flagging intentional silence. The trade-off is higher curation load from false positives like ASMR or soundscapes, but ingestion’s auto-flagging keeps the net impact low.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s "untranscribed" flag risks flooding curation with false positives—ASMR, ambient noise, or non-English speech that ingestion *could* transcribe with better models. Better: route only videos where ingestion *explicitly fails* to extract *any* transcriptable audio (silence, corruption, or non-speech) to curation, and let ingestion auto-flag the rest. Settle it by testing both rules against a labeled dataset of 1,000 videos and measuring false positives vs. missed unusable uploads.

name: Scope
text: Route videos where ingestion fails to extract *any* transcriptable audio—silence, corruption, or non-English speech—to curation immediately. This catches the widest range of unusable uploads early, reducing wasted processing on untranscribable content. The trade-off is higher curation load from false positives like ASMR or ambient noise, but ingestion’s failure flag is the most reliable indicator of unusable audio.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s "no transcriptable audio" rule misses videos where ingestion *partially* fails—e.g., transcribes only 5 seconds of a 10-minute video with corrupted audio. That wastes processing on untranscribable content while still letting some unusable videos slip through. Instead, route videos where ingestion flags *any* transcript failure (partial or full) to curation, and let curators decide severity. Settle it by testing both rules on a week of uploads and measuring wasted processing vs. missed unusable videos.

name: Reel
text: Route videos where ingestion *fails to extract any transcriptable audio at all*—silence, corruption, or non-English speech—to curation immediately. This catches the widest range of unusable uploads early, cutting wasted processing on untranscribable content. The trade-off is higher curation load from false positives like ASMR or ambient noise, but it’s the cleanest filter for unusable audio.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s "no transcriptable audio at all" rule still lets videos with *partial* transcription slip through—wasting processing on unusable content while missing edge cases. Instead, route videos where ingestion extracts **less than 10% of expected transcript length** to curation; this catches partial failures without overloading curation. Settle it with a 1-week test: measure false positives (ASMR, ambient noise) and false negatives (corrupted audio) before scaling.

name: Chisel
text: Route videos where ingestion extracts **less than 10% of expected transcript length** directly to curation. This catches partial failures—like 5 seconds transcribed in a 10-minute video—without over-flagging ASMR or ambient noise. The trade-off is accepting some false positives where short but valid content (e.g., a 30-second clip) gets routed unnecessarily. Curation will handle the rest.

name: Sift
text: The "less than 10% transcript" rule still risks misclassifying legitimate short-form content as failures—think 30-second product demos or 1-minute tutorials. Instead, route videos where ingestion extracts **zero transcriptable audio** *or* the transcript length is **less than 5% of expected duration**—this cuts false positives while catching partial failures. Settle it by testing both thresholds on a week’s worth of uploads and measuring wasted processing vs. missed unusable videos.

name: Scope
text: Route videos where ingestion extracts **zero transcriptable audio** *or* the transcript is **less than 5% of expected duration** directly to curation. This catches all partial failures—like 5 seconds in a 10-minute video—while minimizing false positives for short-form content. The trade-off is accepting some legitimate short videos (e.g., 30-second demos) getting routed unnecessarily, but the cost is lower than processing untranscribable bulk.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 5% rule still lets through videos where ingestion *partially* fails—like 30 seconds transcribed in a 20-minute video—wasting processing on unusable content. Instead, route videos where ingestion extracts **less than 10% of expected transcript length** *and* the video duration exceeds 5 minutes; this catches partial failures without misclassifying short-form content. Settle it by testing both rules on a 10,000-video sample and measuring wasted processing vs. false positives.

name: Reel
text: Route videos where ingestion extracts **less than 10% of expected transcript length** *and* the video duration exceeds **5 minutes** directly to curation. This catches partial failures—like 30 seconds transcribed in a 20-minute video—without misclassifying short-form content. The trade-off is accepting some false negatives where long videos with minimal speech (e.g., ambient footage) slip through, but it’s the sharpest balance between precision and efficiency.

name: Scriv
text: The 5-minute duration threshold is arbitrary and will miss long-form failures under 5 minutes. Instead, enforce the 10% transcript rule universally—no duration gate—then let curation manually override false positives for short-form content. Settle it by running a 30-day A/B test: compare false positive rates and missed failure rates between the two rules.

name: Chisel
text: Run a 30-day A/B test comparing two curation routing rules: (A) route videos with **less than 10% transcript length** directly to curation, and (B) route videos with **zero transcriptable audio** or **less than 5% transcript length**. The test will measure false positives for short-form content and missed failures for long-form videos. Trade-off: Accept temporary inefficiency from false positives to gather data that will refine the rule permanently.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s A/B test risks conflating two variables—transcript length thresholds *and* curation overrides—so it won’t isolate which rule drives the difference. Instead, run a 30-day test comparing (A) **10% threshold only** vs. (B) **5% threshold only**, both with identical manual override rules, and measure false positives for short-form content and long-form failures. If (B) cuts long-form waste without spiking short-form errors, adopt it; otherwise, default to (A).

name: Scope
text: Route all videos with **less than 10% transcript length** directly to curation, no duration gate. This catches every partial failure—even 30 seconds in a 20-minute video—without arbitrary cutoffs. The trade-off is more false positives for short-form content, but curation can manually override those.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 10% rule alone will drown curation in false positives from short-form content—like a 30-second TikTok with 3 seconds transcribed. Instead, enforce the 10% rule only for videos over 2 minutes, then let curation manually review the rest. Settle it with a 30-day A/B test: compare false positives and manual override rates between the two rules.

name: Reel
text: Route all videos with **less than 10% transcript length** directly to curation, no duration gate. This catches every partial failure—even 30 seconds in a 20-minute video—without arbitrary cutoffs. The trade-off is more false positives for short-form content, but curation can manually override those.

name: Scriv
text: The 10% rule without a duration gate still risks flooding curation with short-form false positives—like a 10-second meme with 1 second transcribed—while missing long-form failures under 10%. Instead, enforce the 10% rule only for videos over 1 minute, then route anything shorter to manual review by default. Settle it with a 30-day A/B test: compare false positives and missed failures between the two rules.

name: Chisel
text: Run a 30-day A/B test comparing (A) the 10% transcript rule for all videos vs. (B) the 10% rule only for videos over 1 minute, with manual review for anything shorter. This isolates the false-positive cost of short-form content without conflating rules. The trade-off is accepting a small delay for sub-minute videos while measuring whether the duration gate meaningfully reduces curation load.

name: Sift
text: The real risk in Chisel’s 30-day A/B test is that it still conflates two variables: transcript length thresholds *and* duration gates. A better alternative is to test (A) **10% threshold for all videos** vs. (B) **10% threshold for all videos *plus* a 2-minute duration gate**, then measure false positives and missed failures separately. Settle it by running the test for 30 days and comparing curation load vs. failure detection rates—no manual overrides allowed in either arm.

name: Scope
text: Do the 10% transcript rule for all videos, no duration gate. This catches every partial failure—even 3-second clips with 0.3 seconds transcribed—without arbitrary cutoffs. The trade-off is more false positives for short-form content, but curation can manually override those.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 10% rule for all videos drowns curation in false positives from short-form content—like a 10-second meme with 1 second transcribed—while missing long-form failures under 10%. Instead, enforce the 10% rule only for videos over 1 minute, then route anything shorter to manual review by curation. Settle it with a 30-day A/B test: compare false positives and missed failures between the two approaches.

name: Reel
text: Enforce the **10% transcript rule only for videos over 1 minute**, routing anything shorter to manual curation review. This cuts false positives from short-form content—like 10-second memes with 1 second transcribed—while still catching long-form failures under 10%. The trade-off is a small delay for short videos, but curation’s manual override keeps quality high without arbitrary cutoffs.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s plan still conflates transcript coverage with duration—what about a 10-second clip with 100% transcribed but 0% relevant content? Instead, test (A) **10% transcript rule for all videos** vs. (B) **10% transcript rule *plus* a 2-minute duration gate *plus* a 30% semantic relevance threshold**—then measure false positives *and* missed failures. The artifact: a 30-day A/B test report signed by curation and transcripts leads.
